title: Security 101
subtitle: A practical survey of how digital systems fail, how to reduce risk, and how to respond when controls fail.
summary: A beginner course for building a useful map of cybersecurity. Learn the shared language and everyday decisions used across software, IT, and cloud security without pretending to train for a specialist role.
pace: 1–2 weeks at 3–4 hours per week, or at your own pace
audience: People who work with or are curious about software and computer systems: developers, IT learners, students, and career explorers.
scope: This course builds breadth: security concepts, systems, networks, identity, common application risks, and basic response. It does not teach penetration testing, production cloud administration, incident command, or specialist certification objectives.
completion: Complete the 12 lessons, pass each knowledge check, finish each in-course activity, and submit the final service review. Learning is free; an optional certificate fee must be disclosed before purchase.

units.title: 1. The security mindset
units.description: Build a practical vocabulary for assets, threats, controls, and risk.

lessons.title: What are we trying to protect?
lessons.summary: Start with the purpose of security: protect something valuable while helping a system do its job.
notes: Security is a set of decisions about what a system should allow, what it should resist, and how people will recover when something goes wrong. It is not a product you install once. A secure service still needs to be usable, maintained, and monitored.

The CIA model is a useful first lens. Confidentiality means information is seen only by intended people or systems. Integrity means information and behavior stay accurate and trustworthy. Availability means authorized users can use the service when they need it. One design decision can help one goal while hurting another, so teams must understand the service’s purpose.

For a file-sharing service, private documents need confidentiality, approvals need integrity, and reviewers need availability. These goals help make vague claims such as “make it secure” more concrete. Ask what could be exposed, changed, or interrupted, and whose work would be affected.

Security is also a human and organizational concern. A control that people cannot understand may be bypassed; a control with no owner may quietly stop working. Good security makes safer behavior the ordinary path and gives the team a way to notice and correct failures.

quiz.question: A document service prevents unauthorized users from reading private reports. Which security goal is it mainly protecting?
options: Confidentiality
Availability
Integrity
quiz.explanation: Confidentiality limits who can see information. Availability and integrity address different risks.

practice.title: Security goals map
practice.prompt: A clinic scheduling service stores patient details and appointment times. Choose the best match for each concern: a stranger reads the details; an attacker changes an appointment; the service is down during check-in.
options: Confidentiality; integrity; availability
Availability; confidentiality; integrity
Integrity; availability; confidentiality
practice.explanation: Map the harm before choosing controls: exposure affects confidentiality, unauthorized changes affect integrity, and downtime affects availability.
reflection: Which of confidentiality, integrity, or availability matters most to the patient in this example, and why?
Describe one realistic way an appointment could be changed by mistake or abuse.
Name one signal the clinic could monitor to notice a serious failure.

resources.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0

resources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0

lessons.title: Threats, weaknesses, and risk
lessons.summary: Learn to describe security problems as a plausible path to a meaningful outcome.
notes: An asset is something worth protecting: data, accounts, money, service capacity, or trust. A threat is a possible cause of harm, such as a stolen credential, a mistake, a software defect, or a power failure. A vulnerability is a weakness that could help a threat cause harm.

Risk connects a scenario to its consequences. Instead of saying “the database is risky,” describe a path: a public endpoint accepts an unvalidated file name; an attacker changes the path; the service reads a private file; customer records are exposed. This statement gives a team something to investigate and fix.

Risk ratings are estimates, not measurements of truth. Likelihood, impact, exposure, and existing controls can help teams compare scenarios, but a red or green label does not replace the reasoning behind it. Write down assumptions and revisit them when evidence changes.

Prioritize consequences and reachable paths. A dramatic but unreachable scenario may matter less than a simple failure on a public, frequently used feature. Security work is a sequence of choices under limited time, so explaining why a risk matters is part of the technical work.

quiz.question: Which statement is a useful risk scenario?
options: The application has vulnerabilities
A public upload endpoint may let an unauthenticated user overwrite another customer’s file
Security is important
quiz.explanation: A useful scenario names a path, an actor or cause, and a concrete impact.

practice.title: Turn a vague concern into a scenario
practice.prompt: A team says, “Our admin area is risky.” Which follow-up gives the clearest starting point for assessment?
options: Which action, identity, or data could be reached through the admin area, and what would happen if access were misused?
Can we buy a scanner today?
Can we mark the concern low so the release can continue?
practice.explanation: Clarifying the asset, access path, and consequence turns a vague concern into a scenario that can be tested.
reflection: Write one concrete risk scenario for an admin page, including a path and a possible consequence.
What evidence would help you estimate how exposed the feature is?
Name one assumption in your scenario that you would verify with the team.

resources.title: NIST CSF 2.0 Quick-Start Guides

resources.title: OWASP Top 10

lessons.title: Trust boundaries and simple threat models
lessons.summary: Trace where assumptions change between people, devices, services, and data stores.
notes: A trust boundary is a place where data or authority crosses between components with different assumptions. Examples include a browser calling an API, one service calling another, or an application reading a file supplied by a user. Boundaries deserve attention because inputs and identity claims can be wrong or manipulated.

A small threat model can be made with four questions: what are we building; what matters to protect; where are the trust boundaries; and how could the design fail? A simple box-and-arrow sketch is often enough to start. Label users, services, data stores, and the direction of important data flows.

For every flow, ask what arrives, who controls it, how identity is established, and what the receiving component checks. A signed-in user is not automatically trusted for every action. A service should check permission close to the protected operation, using an identity and policy it can trust.

Threat modeling is not a prediction exercise. It helps a team notice assumptions early and choose a few controls to validate. Keep the model small, record what is out of scope, and update it when the architecture or the way people use the system changes.

quiz.question: Why is a browser-to-server connection a useful place to mark a trust boundary?
options: The server receives data and claims from a component it does not control
The browser always sends correct information
The boundary means the network is encrypted
quiz.explanation: A server must treat client input as untrusted and verify it. Encryption protects a connection but does not make a client trustworthy.

practice.title: Threat-model workbench
practice.prompt: A learner uploads a document that a reviewer can approve and an administrator can publish. Which first diagram is most useful?
options: Learner browser → upload service → document store; reviewer and administrator identities shown with their separate actions
A list of security products the company owns
Only the public home page, because the rest is internal
practice.explanation: The data flow and separate roles reveal trust boundaries and help the team ask who can upload, approve, and publish.
reflection: List two valuable assets in the document workflow and why each matters.
Describe one trust boundary and what untrusted input crosses it.
Write one abuse case and one control you would validate.

units.title: 2. Systems, networks, and identity
units.description: Understand the basic pieces that security controls act on.

lessons.title: Computers, processes, and permissions
lessons.summary: See how programs run and why users and permissions limit what a compromised process can do.
notes: An operating system coordinates hardware and gives programs shared ways to use memory, storage, networks, and devices. A running program is a process. Processes execute with an identity and permissions, so the identity attached to a service can strongly affect the damage a bug can cause.

Files commonly have an owner and rules that distinguish reading, changing, and executing. The exact permission model varies by system, but the security idea is broadly useful: grant only the access needed for a task. A report generator that only reads reports should not be able to change payroll records or administer the whole computer.

Accounts, groups, service identities, and operating-system permissions are controls around the process. Running routine programs with administrator privileges removes an important boundary. Separate identities also make it easier to understand which component performed an action.

When investigating a system, ask which process handled the request, which identity it used, what files and network destinations it could reach, and where its logs go. These questions are useful even before a learner knows command-line syntax or a specific operating system.

quiz.question: A report process only needs to read one directory. What is a sound starting permission?
options: Run as the system administrator
Give its dedicated identity read access to that directory only
Make every directory writable by every user
quiz.explanation: A narrowly scoped service identity limits the impact of a defect or compromise.

practice.title: Permission design sandbox
practice.prompt: Choose access for a service that creates a daily summary from /srv/reports and should not alter source files.
options: Dedicated identity with read-only access to the required reports and write access only to its output folder
Root access to the entire host
Shared human account with access to all company folders
practice.explanation: Separate source and output access, and use a dedicated identity to reduce privilege and improve accountability.
reflection: What files must this service read, and where should it be allowed to write?
If the process were compromised, what damage could still occur under your permission plan?
What log entry would help connect an action to this service identity?

lessons.title: How a web request reaches a service
lessons.summary: Follow a request through names, network connections, HTTP, and TLS.
notes: A browser starts with a name such as learn.example. DNS provides records that help it find a network destination. IP addresses identify endpoints at the network layer; ports help a machine deliver traffic to the right service. DNS answers can be cached, so the lookup is not necessarily repeated for every request.

Transport protocols provide ways to move data between endpoints. TCP establishes an ordered connection; UDP sends datagrams without the same connection behavior. Applications use these transports according to their needs. Firewalls and network rules can limit which endpoints are reachable, but an open connection does not tell us whether an application action is authorized.

HTTP describes requests and responses. A request includes a method, path, headers, and sometimes a body. A response includes a status code, headers, and possibly content. Cookies can carry session identifiers; headers can influence behavior. Servers must validate incoming values because clients control much of what they send.

HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS. TLS helps protect data in transit and authenticate the server name using certificates. It does not prove that the service is free of vulnerabilities, and it does not protect a user from an authorized account being misused. Security controls need to exist at multiple layers.

quiz.question: What does TLS mainly add to a browser connection to a web service?
options: Protection of data in transit and a way to authenticate the server
A guarantee that the application has no flaws
A check that every user is authorized for every action
quiz.explanation: TLS protects the connection and helps authenticate the server; application security and authorization remain separate responsibilities.

practice.title: Trace the request
practice.prompt: A learner opens an HTTPS course page. Which sequence best describes the browser reaching it?
options: Enter the name, resolve it with DNS, establish TLS to the server, send the HTTPS request
Send the protected HTTP request, then discover the server using DNS
Use TLS to authorize the learner to publish course content
practice.explanation: Name resolution precedes connecting to the destination; TLS protects the connection, while application authorization decides what the learner may do.
reflection: Describe what DNS contributes to this request and one thing DNS does not prove.
Name two pieces of an HTTP request that the server should treat carefully.
What protection does TLS provide, and what application risk remains after TLS is enabled?

lessons.title: Identity, authentication, and authorization
lessons.summary: Separate proving who someone is from deciding what they can do.
notes: Identification is the claim of an identity; authentication checks evidence for that claim; authorization decides which actions are allowed. These are related but distinct steps. A successful sign-in should not automatically give a user broad access to data or administrative actions.

Passwords are one authentication factor and can be guessed, reused, or stolen. Multi-factor authentication asks for evidence from another category, such as possession of a registered device. MFA reduces some account-takeover risks, but recovery processes and session theft still need consideration.

Authorization can be based on roles, attributes, relationships, or a combination. Whatever model is used, the policy should be clear and enforced where the protected action occurs. Hiding an interface control is not enough: a client can be modified or a request sent directly.

A good access design states who may do what to which resource under what conditions. Use separate roles for distinct duties, avoid shared accounts, review permissions over time, and log sensitive changes. Think about how an account is created, changed, recovered, disabled, and audited—not only how it signs in.

quiz.question: A user can sign in successfully but must not approve their own document. Which decision enforces that rule?
options: Authentication
Authorization
DNS resolution
quiz.explanation: Authentication establishes an identity; authorization decides whether that identity may perform the approval.

practice.title: Access-control sandbox
practice.prompt: Use the sample app to see why a server must verify permission instead of trusting a role claim supplied by the browser.
reflection: What did the vulnerable demo trust, and why could the learner change it?
Where should the authorization decision happen in a real publish request?
Name one test case that should deny access and one that should allow it.

units.title: 3. Building safer software and services
units.description: Recognize common application risks and practical design responses.

lessons.title: Untrusted input and injection
lessons.summary: Understand how data becomes dangerous when software mistakes it for instructions.
notes: Applications receive input from browsers, APIs, files, queues, and other services. A value may be malformed, unexpected, or deliberately chosen to affect application behavior. Validate that input matches the intended type, size, and format, but do not treat validation as the only defense.

Injection happens when a program combines data with an instruction language in a way that lets the data change the instruction. SQL injection is one example: an unsafe query can interpret user-supplied text as part of the database command. Similar design mistakes occur with shell commands, templates, and other interpreters.

Parameterized queries keep data separate from SQL instructions. Safe APIs and context-aware output encoding serve similar goals in other contexts. Escaping rules differ by destination, so hand-written filters often miss edge cases. Prefer well-maintained libraries and APIs that preserve the code/data boundary.

Errors should help developers diagnose a problem without revealing secrets or internal details to an attacker. Tests should include ordinary, boundary, and malformed input. The deeper lesson is to identify where data crosses into a language or privileged operation, then use a design that keeps it data.

quiz.question: What is the core reason parameterized database queries help prevent SQL injection?
options: They keep supplied values separate from query instructions
They encrypt every database record
They prevent users from submitting any input
quiz.explanation: Separating values from SQL structure prevents input from changing the meaning of the query.

practice.title: Safer query design
practice.prompt: A search endpoint inserts a supplied name directly into a SQL string. Which change most directly addresses the design flaw?
options: Use a parameterized query and validate the expected input type
Hide the search box with CSS
Block only the characters seen in one example attack
practice.explanation: Parameterized queries preserve the boundary between data and instructions; validation adds an appropriate input constraint.
reflection: In your own words, describe how data could become part of a database instruction.
What is one reason a hand-written blocklist can fail?
Name one test input you would include to check the query boundary safely.

resources.title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

lessons.title: Sessions and access control in web apps
lessons.summary: Explore how a signed-in browser keeps a session and how the server should enforce permissions.
notes: HTTP requests are independent, so applications commonly use a session identifier to associate requests with a signed-in user. That identifier acts like a temporary bearer credential: someone who steals it may be able to act as the user until it expires or is revoked.

Session cookies should be protected with appropriate attributes. Secure limits transmission to HTTPS, HttpOnly prevents ordinary browser scripts from reading the cookie, and SameSite can reduce some cross-site request risks. Cookie settings do not replace authorization checks or protection against all cross-site attacks.

Authorization must be checked for each protected operation, using the authenticated identity and the resource being accessed. A route may require an administrator role, while a document operation may additionally require ownership or reviewer assignment. Default-deny behavior helps ensure that unlisted cases do not become allowed accidentally.

Cross-site request forgery exploits a browser’s automatic use of credentials in some situations. Defenses depend on the application, but may include anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, origin checks, and requiring re-authentication for sensitive actions. Security controls should match the actual threat and be tested at the server boundary.

quiz.question: Where should a permission check for publishing a document happen?
options: Only in the browser before showing the Publish button
On the server for the publish operation
In a comment beside the user interface
quiz.explanation: The server controls the protected action and must verify permission each time it is requested.

practice.title: Review the publish flow
practice.prompt: A learner edits a request in browser tools and changes documentId to another learner’s file. What control should stop the publish operation?
options: The server verifies this identity may publish that specific document
The page uses a hidden button
The document identifier is hard to guess
practice.explanation: Unpredictable identifiers and hidden controls are not authorization. The server must check the identity’s rights to the requested resource.
reflection: Write the authorization rule for publishing one approved document.
Which account and resource attributes must the server verify before the action?
What negative test would prove that one learner cannot act on another learner’s document?

lessons.title: Data protection, secrets, and encryption
lessons.summary: Choose sensible protections for data at rest, data in transit, and credentials used by services.
notes: Start data protection by asking what information the service truly needs, where it moves, who uses it, and how long it remains useful. Collecting less sensitive data reduces what can be exposed. Retention and deletion policies are security controls as well as operational decisions.

Encryption transforms data so it is not readily readable without the appropriate key. Encryption in transit protects a connection; encryption at rest can protect stored media when an underlying storage layer is accessed. Neither form decides which application user is allowed to read the decrypted data.

Keys and secrets need their own protections: limit who and what can access them, avoid putting them in source code or logs, rotate them when exposed, and use a managed secret store or workload identity where available. A secret that many people and services share is difficult to audit and revoke safely.

Passwords should be stored using a password-hashing design intended for that purpose, not reversible encryption or plain text. Applications should use established cryptographic libraries and protocols rather than inventing algorithms. Security depends on key management and correct use, not on an algorithm name alone.

quiz.question: What does encryption at rest fail to decide by itself?
options: Whether an authenticated application user is authorized to read a particular record
Whether stored bytes are transformed cryptographically
Whether a storage medium is physically present
quiz.explanation: Encryption protects data in certain access scenarios, but the application still needs authorization and safe key handling.

practice.title: Secret-handling review
practice.prompt: A developer accidentally commits a cloud API key to a public repository. What is the strongest response?
options: Revoke or rotate the exposed key, investigate its use, and move secrets to an appropriate managed mechanism
Delete the visible line and assume the old key is safe
Rename the key so scanners cannot find it
practice.explanation: A published credential should be considered compromised; remove its authority and investigate before establishing safer storage.
reflection: Why is deleting the key from the latest source version not enough?
What evidence would you inspect to determine whether the key was used?
Describe a safer way for the service to receive the credential it needs.

units.title: 4. Operating securely and responding
units.description: Connect basic controls, useful evidence, and a final security review.

lessons.title: Secure defaults, updates, and dependencies
lessons.summary: See how routine engineering choices reduce common exposure before an incident occurs.
notes: Secure defaults make the safer configuration the easiest one to deploy. Examples include private-by-default storage, narrow service permissions, strong session settings, and disabling features that are not needed. Teams should know which defaults can be changed and how changes are reviewed.

Updates correct defects, including security defects, in operating systems, applications, libraries, and devices. A team needs an inventory of important components, a way to assess relevant updates, and a deployment plan that considers urgency and service risk. “We will patch later” is not a process unless later has an owner and a deadline.

Modern applications depend on third-party packages and base images. Track what is used, prefer maintained sources, review high-impact changes, and remove unused components. Automated dependency alerts are useful signals but need a response process and a way to confirm which products are affected.

Backups, recovery procedures, and configuration review help limit the cost of mistakes. A backup that has never been restored is only an assumption. Periodically test restore steps, understand who can alter backup copies, and include recovery time in service planning.

quiz.question: What makes a secure default valuable?
options: It makes a safer configuration the normal starting point
It removes the need for testing and updates
It guarantees no user can make a mistake
quiz.explanation: Good defaults reduce avoidable exposure while still requiring maintenance and review.

practice.title: Release readiness check
practice.prompt: A service release adds an unused debug endpoint and uses an old library with a known fix available. What is the best next step?
options: Disable the unnecessary endpoint and plan a tested dependency update before release
Ship first and rely on encryption
Leave the endpoint available but rename it
practice.explanation: Remove unnecessary exposure and update the affected component through a reviewed, tested change.
reflection: Which unnecessary service or feature would you disable, and how would you confirm it is unused?
What would you check before updating the vulnerable dependency?
Who should own the update deadline and how will completion be verified?

lessons.title: Logs, alerts, and the first hour of an incident
lessons.summary: Know what evidence is useful and how to respond without destroying it.
notes: Logs record events that help explain what a system did. Useful security records often include sign-ins, permission changes, important administrative actions, service errors, and changes to sensitive data. Decide which questions the logs should answer before collecting everything indiscriminately.

A log needs context: a timestamp, a consistent identity, the action, the target resource, and a result where possible. Protect logs from unauthorized changes and access, avoid recording passwords or tokens, and make sure clock differences do not make the timeline misleading.

An alert is a signal to investigate, not proof of a breach. Confirm the event, compare it with expected behavior, gather related evidence, and record what is known and unknown. Preserve relevant records before changes erase or rotate them.

Response is coordinated work. The first actions may include limiting an active threat, protecting people and data, preserving evidence, and contacting the responsible team. The right sequence depends on impact and urgency. After recovery, record decisions and improve controls, runbooks, and detections based on what was learned.

quiz.question: An alert reports an unfamiliar administrator sign-in. What is a sound initial response?
options: Validate the event, preserve related records, and begin a timeline
Delete the logs to stop further alerts
Assume the alert proves who attacked the system
quiz.explanation: Validation and evidence preservation support a careful investigation and proportionate response.

practice.title: Incident response tabletop
practice.prompt: A new administrator account appears just before a sensitive storage policy changes. Which immediate work best supports a safe response?
options: Preserve identity and audit records, validate who made the changes, assess current exposure, and coordinate containment
Publish the suspected employee’s name and delete the account logs
Wait for more alerts before checking whether sensitive data is public
practice.explanation: Preserve evidence and establish scope while the responsible team evaluates containment and user impact.
reflection: What facts would you add to the first incident timeline?
Which records and people could help confirm the account’s activity?
Name one immediate containment option and a possible side effect to consider.

lessons.title: Final exercise: review a small service
lessons.summary: Use the course vocabulary to make a concise, evidence-based security review.
notes: Use this fictional service: learners upload documents; reviewers approve them; administrators publish approved documents; the service stores files and sends email notifications. State that your review covers this flow only. A useful review has a boundary, assumptions, and an explicit list of things it did not assess.

Identify assets and goals. Consider private documents, user identities, approval decisions, service availability, and notification contents. Mark the browser-to-service and service-to-storage boundaries, and note which roles can perform each action.

Write a few concrete abuse or failure cases. For example, a learner changes a document identifier and reads another learner’s file; a notification accidentally includes a private download link; or a stolen reviewer session is used to approve a malicious upload. Choose cases based on impact and plausible paths.

For each prioritized case, name a control and evidence that would help verify it. Server-side resource authorization can be checked with tests using two learner accounts. Private object storage can be reviewed in configuration. Audit records can be checked for actor, action, resource, outcome, and timestamp.

Finish with a short report: summary, scope, assumptions, findings with evidence and impact, recommended fixes, and one remaining uncertainty. A good beginner review is honest about what was and was not checked. It does not claim a system is completely secure.

quiz.question: Which final review finding is most useful to an engineering team?
options: A reproducible test shows learner A can read learner B’s document by changing an ID; enforce ownership on the server
The system feels unsafe
Install several security tools
quiz.explanation: A clear reproduction, concrete impact, and implementable fix make a finding actionable.

practice.title: Security review decision
practice.prompt: Select the review plan that best applies Security 101 without claiming specialist depth.
options: State scope, map roles and data flows, test one high-impact access rule, document evidence and a practical fix
Run an unapproved attack against a real service and declare it secure if nothing breaks
List every security term from the course without connecting it to the service
practice.explanation: A bounded review with evidence and an honest limitation demonstrates useful security reasoning without overclaiming.
reflection: Define the scope and one important assumption for the fictional review.
Write one finding with a reproduction, impact, and practical recommendation.
What did your review not test, and what deeper follow-up would you recommend?
